transcript: Dylan Mulvaney knows her very existence is considered controversial by many, but to her, she's the least problematic woman in the world. Her solo show, currently running at the Lucille Lortel Theatre in the West Village, is a satirical and autobiographical romp through the most defining moments in her journey to womanhood. Specific in theme but comprehensive in scope, she takes us from her childhood as a Catholic schoolboy all the way through an ill-fated sponsorship deal with a beer company in her early adulthood. In addition to having an interesting story to tell, Dylan has a warmth and charisma that hooks you from the start and doesn't let up. As she joked, sang, and sashayed her way through her story, I was struck by a sense of nostalgia I felt she brought to some of her early memories. I think there's something really beautiful about finding levity and nuance in what must have been a painful and confusing chapter. It's this level of specificity and depth that makes the piece feel emotionally grounded and genuine, even with its plethora of pop culture and queer references which not many performers would be able to pull off. And overall, specificity is Dylan's greatest weapon in this piece, and she cleverly resists the generalizations about trans women that so many people have tried to saddle her with. She's one person, and she's telling one person’s story. The Least Problematic Woman In The World is running through October 19th — don't miss it. With that, another program for my collection.
